content.title: What is a Blue Alert? Emergency notification sent after Greensboro officer was shot explained
content.text: Saturday night around 6 p.m., every North Carolinian who has on emergency alerts in their phone settings, heard the alert from their phone. The emergency alert read, "NC BLUE ALERT Assault on Law Enforcement Officer - Greensboro NC - KKA - 4332 (NC) Black Chevrolet Equinox, Last Seen West from Greensboro on I-40." Morrissa Moyer, the director for the North Carolina Center for Missing Persons, said it's the first Blue Alert they've ever had to active in the state. Moyer said she sent the blue alert shortly after Sgt. Philip Dale Nix was shot. “There's that initial heartbreak for the law enforcement agency, for their telecommunicators and, of course, for the family. Then the next thought was, we have to get this out, we have to get this out right now," Moyer said. What is a Blue Alert?Blue Alerts were created in 2015 when former President Barack Obama signed it into law. North Carolina adopted the Blue Alert Notification System in 2016 when North Carolina Gov. Pat McCrory signed it into law. According to the NC Center of Missing Persons, the law was named in honor of two New York City Police Detectives who were killed while sitting in their patrol car in 2014. “It's made specifically for when a law enforcement officer is seriously injured or killed, and the suspects are on the loose," Moyer said.Currently, 27 states have implemented the Blue Alert system to go along with the other alerts that are very well known, like Amber and Silver alerts. “They’re our eyes for the entire state. The general public is able to reach out and see more than even all of the law enforcement officers on the road just because of the sheer volume of numbers," Moyer said.Watch: NOWCAST streaming newscastsHow does a Blue Alert work?Moyer said after an incident happens, a law enforcement agency will contact the NC Center for Missing Persons and request a Blue Alert. The center will then approve it. There's certain criteria required before a Blue Alert can be sent out. A law enforcement officer is killed or suffers a serious injury. A law enforcement agency determines the suspect responsible poses a threat to the public and other law enforcement.The head of a law enforcement agency recommends the Blue Alert.The NC Center for Missing Persons then contacts the State Highway Patrol Troop C Communication Center in Raleigh with instructions on how to issue an Emergency Alert System message on signs on highways. How does a Blue Alert compare to other alerts? The NC Center of Missing Persons is in charge of sending all of the state's alerts, including Silver, AMBER, Blue, Missing Endangered and Ashanti.Silver Alert Issued when an elderly individual with dementia/Alzheimer's is missingEndangered Alert Issued when someone with a cognitive impairment is missing Amber Alert Issued when a child is abducted and is in danger Ashanti AlertIssued when an adult has been abductedBlue AlertIssued when a law enforcement officer is killed or injured and the suspect is on the looseKeep up with the latest news and weather by downloading the WXII app here.The alert was canceled just hours after Moyer initially sent it out. Moyer said some people reported getting the alert twice. She said that's due to background technical issues and cellphone provider issues.She said hopefully they don't have to send out another one in the future, but said she hopes more people are more aware of what a Blue Alert is now."If we send something out to your handset, you know, keep your eyes open. If you see something, don't be hesitate to call 911," Moyer said.
